How cognitive behavioral therapy works to treat OCD

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next.
  • What unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next. For some people, it’s checking the locks again and again, even when they know the door is shut. For others, it’s washing their hands until they feel clean, counting steps or objects, arranging things until they feel just right, or getting stuck on an unwanted thought.

What unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop. But the relief doesn’t last and you end up back at the anxious thought, triggering the process again. For people living with OCD, this cycle can be exhausting.

According to recent reports, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most studied ways to break the OCD cycle, and one type in particular, called exposure and response prevention (ERP), has the strongest research support of any talk therapy for OCD. Here’s a look at what CBT for OCD involves, how ERP works, and what a session can feel like.

In a recent development, CBT is a structured, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It looks at how your thoughts, feelings, and actions feed each other, and it focuses on the present rather than digging through your past. Most versions help you notice unhelpful thoughts and respond to them in fresh ways.

CBT for OCD works a little differently. With something like anxiety or low mood, a therapist might help you question a worried thought and look for more balanced evidence. With OCD, that technique can backfire. Trying to argue with an intrusive thought, or prove it wrong, can become a mental compulsion, which keeps the cycle going.

So OCD-focused CBT spends less time debating the content of your thoughts and more time changing how you respond to them. The main tool for that is ERP, a type of CBT that focuses on behavior.

Industry observers note that if you've ever been told to "just stop worrying," you may know that advice doesn’t work for OCD. The cycle doesn’t respond to willpower alone.

Here's how the loop tends to run:.

You get an intrusive thought or fear you don’t want (the obsession).

To get relief, you do something to make the feeling go away (the compulsion), like checking, washing, asking for reassurance, or going over events in your mind.

You feel better, but only for a short while.

It has been revealed that each compulsion can teach your brain that the thought was a true threat and that the ritual kept you safe. So the thought tends to return.

Say you’re leaving for work. A thought pops up: What if I left the stove on? Your anxiety spikes, so you go back and check. The stove is off, and you feel relief. But on your way to the car, the doubt returns, along with the urge to check again.

According to recent reports, that's why OCD can feel impossible to overcome. The very thing that calms you in the moment is what feeds the cycle.

According to recent reports, ERP involves gradually facing the things that trigger your fears, while holding off on the compulsion. It can sound intimidating, but it’s planned and step by step, and you and your therapist agree on each move together. Here’s what it tends to look like.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of questions up front: Early sessions are mostly about getting clear on what's happening. Expect to talk through your intrusive thoughts, the compulsions they trigger, and the situations you avoid.

Recent findings suggest that building a fear ladder: Your triggers get ranked from mild to most distressing, and you start near the bottom. You won't be asked to face your worst fear on day one.

Facing triggers on purpose: You'll meet a fear instead of dodging it, whether that's touching a doorknob, writing down a feared word, or sitting with an uncertain thought.

Not doing the compulsion: Expect to resist the response you'd normally reach for, even something subtle like seeking reassurance.

Sitting with the discomfort: At first the fear climbs, which can feel like proof it won't stop. Over time, many people find the fear eases, and they learn they can cope with it.

Homework between sessions: Practice between sessions is a big part of progress, so expect to take exposures home and work on them in your daily life.

ERP with a trained therapist is the core of OCD treatment, and nothing below replaces it. But the stretches between sessions can be long, and a few grounding habits may make them easier to deal with.

Industry observers note that mindfulness and meditation can help you practice noticing a thought, letting it pass, and not acting on it or trying to prove it wrong. That fits well with ERP, where you also learn to let urges be present without giving in. A few minutes a day can be a gentle place to start.

One caution: if you catch yourself meditating to “cancel out” a bad thought, that’s the compulsion sneaking back in. The aim is to let thoughts come and go, not to get rid of them.

💙 Practice noticing a thought and letting it pass with Chibs Okereke’s short Working With Thoughts meditation.

In a recent development, when you’re struggling with anxiety or a racing heart, slow breathing can help your body settle. Box breathing is one option, since the even count gives your mind something simple to hold onto.

Recent findings suggest that use it for everyday stress, like after a tough commute or before bed. During an exposure, or when you’re trying to make a thought go away, it can work against ERP, because the point is to practice facing the discomfort. Ask your therapist when it’s okay to use it alongside your ERP practice.

💙 For a tense, jittery day, Panic SOS with Kirat Randhawa uses sight, sound, and touch to help your body settle.

Poor sleep and OCD symptoms often go hand in hand. Research links poor sleep to more intrusive thoughts and harder-to-manage symptoms. Rest may also make it easier to do your ERP practice.

It has been revealed that A steady routine can help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day, and dim the lights and put screens away 30 minutes or so before bed. A warm shower, gentle stretching, or a sleep meditation can help you unwind, and limiting caffeine later in the day may make it easier to fall asleep.

Bedtime can be a hard time for those of us with OCD, as quiet moments can leave room for intrusive thoughts, checking, or reassurance-seeking. If rituals are keeping you up, mention it to your therapist.

💙 Give your mind permission to power down with this Wind Down (for Sleep) session on Calm.

Industry observers note that putting your obsessions, compulsions, and triggers on paper may help you and your therapist spot patterns you’d otherwise miss. Many people find it easiest to jot down a few quick notes each time the loop shows up: what set it off, what thought or fear came up, what you did in response, and how you felt afterward. Over time, you may notice that certain places, times of day, or moods make the cycle more likely.

While you’re mapping the loop, try not to judge yourself or over-analyze your entries.

💙 If you’re struggling to get started, journaling prompts can help.

Recent findings suggest that A walk around the block, a stretch, or a few minutes of dancing in your kitchen can help ease stress and give your body a reset. Pick something that feels possible even on a hard day, and tie it to something you already do, like a few minutes of movement while your coffee brews or after you hang up a call. Doing it at about the same time each day can also help it stick.

One thing to watch for: if movement starts to feel like a ritual, like needing to take a certain number of steps or repeat a routine until it feels “just right,” mention it to your therapist.

💙 Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Walking series turns a short stroll into a chance to notice what’s around you.

Industry observers note that OCD can be isolating. Talking with a friend or family member you trust can remind you that you’re more than your symptoms. If a loved one wants to help, ask your therapist how. Well-meaning support, like answering the same reassurance question again and again, can accidentally keep the cycle going, and a therapist can guide you both.

A peer support group can also help. Reputable OCD organizations run groups where you can meet people doing the same work.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most effective treatments for OCD, especially a type called exposure and response prevention (ERP). Research highlights it can reduce symptoms for many people.

In a recent development, CBT helps by targeting the anxiety cycle that keeps OCD going. Depending on how severe symptoms are, it's used on its own or alongside medication.

Recent findings suggest that exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the best-studied therapy for OCD, but it isn’t the only option. Other approaches include cognitive therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and inference-based CBT (I-CBT). Cognitive therapy helps you examine the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel threatening. ACT focuses on making room for uncomfortable thoughts rather than fighting them. I-CBT targets the reasoning that makes an obsession feel believable. Medication, usually a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, is a separate treatment that can lower the intensity of symptoms. It’s often combined with therapy. A clinician can help you weigh which mix fits your situation.

Recent findings suggest that ERP, or exposure and response prevention, is a type of CBT where you gradually face your triggers while resisting the urge to do a compulsion. It's a first-line treatment for OCD.

Recent findings suggest that each time you sit with a fear and resist the ritual, your brain gets evidence that the feared outcome doesn't arrive and that the distress is survivable. That learning is what loosens OCD's grip. A therapist structures the exposures so they stay challenging without tipping into overwhelming.

Recent findings suggest that the main difference is what each approach targets. Regular CBT often focuses on changing unhelpful thoughts, such as questioning a worry and replacing it with a more balanced one. CBT for OCD focuses on the compulsion.

In a recent development, that’s because, with OCD, the compulsion is what keeps the cycle going. Each time you do the ritual, or try to prove the fear wrong, your brain learns that the thought was a real threat and the ritual kept you safe. In ERP, you face the trigger and hold off on the compulsion. Over time, your brain learns that the feared outcome doesn’t happen and that you can cope with the anxiety without the ritual. Some therapists also work on the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel so threatening, but ERP is the main tool.

Cognitive distortions are unhelpful thinking patterns, and in OCD they often show up as beliefs that make ordinary doubts feel dangerous. Common examples include:.

Feeling responsible for preventing harm, even when it’s unlikely.

Overestimating how likely something bad is to happen.

Thought-action fusion, or believing a thought is as bad as an action.

Struggling with not knowing for sure (intolerance of uncertainty).

Assuming a thought must matter because you had it.

These patterns are common in OCD, and they can fuel the urge to do compulsions. Therapy can help you spot them and loosen their grip.

💙 Find out more about cognitive distortions and how to reframe negative thoughts.

Many people see meaningful improvement from ERP within about 12–20 sessions, which is often three to four months with weekly visits (intensive programs can be faster). Some notice shifts with fewer sessions, especially with regular practice in between.

Timelines vary with symptom severity, how often you practice, and whether medication is part of the strategy. OCD treatment is usually designed to be relatively short-term and skills-based, not open-ended.

You can do some ERP on your own, and self-help books and apps exist for it, but working with a trained therapist is strongly recommended, especially for moderate to severe OCD.

Self-directed ERP can be tricky to get right. It can be easy to accidentally turn an exposure into a subtle compulsion, or to skip the exposures that matter most. A therapist keeps the initiative honest and adjusts it as you go. If therapy isn't available right now, guided self-help from a reputable OCD organization is a safer starting point than going it fully alone.

Sources indicate that mindfulness can support OCD treatment, but it isn't a standalone fix. Research on mindfulness for OCD is promising but mixed, and ERP remains the first-line treatment.

On its own, mindfulness won't switch off intrusive thoughts, and expecting it to can backfire. Its real value is helping you relate to those thoughts differently, which is why it pairs with therapy rather than replacing it. A clinician can point you toward using it in a way that helps.

💙 If you’d like to try it, these tips for practicing mindfulness meditation are a gentle place to start.

#115602. Breaking: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

Breaking: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

📅 18 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues.
  • The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older. Yet experiments in mice suggest that changes in a protein deep inside the brain can influence all three. Restoring that protein, called Menin, improved several signs of aging, while a separate treatment with the amino acid D-serine improved cognition.

Recent findings suggest that the findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues. The work identified a possible connection between brain inflammation, metabolism, and aging throughout the body. Research published since then has added to that picture, while also showing why the supplement findings require careful interpretation.

How a Brain Protein Could Influence Aging.

The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions. It also appears to influence how the body ages. As inflammatory signaling increases in this region, it can contribute to changes both within the brain and in tissues elsewhere in the body.

In a recent development, before the 2023 study, Leng and colleagues had found that Menin helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. That raised an crucial question: Could losing some of this protection help set age-related decline in motion?

It has been revealed that the team found that Menin levels fell with age in certain neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus, an area involved in regulating metabolism. The same decline was not seen in astrocytes and microglia, two types of cells that support and protect the brain. This suggested that the change was specific to particular cells rather than a uniform loss across the region.

To investigate whether Menin loss could actually contribute to aging, rather than simply accompany it, the researchers created conditional knockout mice. These animals were genetically engineered so that Menin could be selectively removed. Reducing Menin in younger mice increased hypothalamic inflammation and brought on several aging-related traits, including lower bone mass, thinner skin, cognitive decline, and a modestly shorter lifespan.

Menin loss also disrupted a chemical pathway important for communication between brain cells. Mice with less Menin had lower levels of D-serine, an amino acid that helps activate receptors involved in learning and memory. These receptors help neurons adjust the strength of their connections, a process essential for storing information.

An enzyme involved in D-serine production (which was in turn regulated by Menin) became less active, reducing the amino acid's supply. The findings suggested that Menin could influence cognition not only through inflammation, but also by helping maintain the chemistry that supports brain signaling.

In a recent development, D-serine is sometimes used as a dietary supplement, but an important distinction can get lost in discussions of food sources. Serine occurs in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts, while the form incorporated into dietary proteins is L-serine. The body can convert L-serine into D-serine, but the two forms are not interchangeable, and eating these foods is not equivalent to receiving the experimental D-serine treatment.

The researchers next tested whether raising Menin levels could improve the condition of elderly (20-month-old) mice. They delivered the gene for Menin into the hypothalamus, allowing cells in that region to produce more of the protein.

Thirty days later, the treated mice had improvements in skin thickness and bone mass, along with better performance on tests of learning, cognition, and balance. The changes were accompanied by higher D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. The study also reported that restoring Menin extended lifespan in the treated mice.

Recent findings suggest that A separate experiment tested a simpler approach: giving mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks. This improved cognitive performance, including in older animals. However, the supplement did not reproduce the broader improvements in physical aging traits seen after Menin restoration. The distinction matters: the study did not show that taking D-serine reversed aging throughout the body.

At the time, Leng described the potential significance of the findings:.

"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline.".

In a recent development, leng added, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

Subsequent studies have explored related mechanisms, although they should not be treated as direct confirmation of the entire Menin aging pathway.

A study published in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry in March 2024 examined Menin in cultured mouse hippocampal cells exposed to the stress hormone corticosterone. A compound called itaconate increased Menin levels and reduced inflammation and a form of cell death. When the researchers silenced Menin, that protection disappeared. The result supported a protective role for Menin in another experimental setting, but it was a cell study, not a demonstration of slower aging in animals or people.

Sources indicate that other work has strengthened the case that communication between the hypothalamus and the rest of the body can influence aging. In a 2024 Cell Metabolism study, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. Interventions that maintained or stimulated this system increased physical activity and extended lifespan in mice. The study involved a different molecular pathway from Menin, but reinforced the broader idea that brain signals can affect aging beyond the brain.

A much larger view emerged in January 2025, when an Allen Institute team reported an analysis of roughly 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature. Some of the cell types most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the hypothalamus's third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity. Many showed reduced activity in genes associated with neuronal function alongside increased activity in genes related to immune responses. That study mapped changes associated with aging rather than testing a treatment, but it highlighted the hypothalamus as an notable area for further investigation.

Why More D-Serine Is Not Necessarily Better.

Later research also complicates the idea that increasing D-serine should always benefit an aging brain.

Sources indicate that in April 2025, a study in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences examined mice engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease. In that model, an early rise in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Genetically removing the enzyme that produces D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive problems. This was a different biological setting from the Menin experiments, but it demonstrated that D-serine can have different effects depending on the underlying disease process.

Research published on September 16, 2026, in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease pointed in another direction. In a different Alzheimer's mouse model, a diet enriched with L-serine increased blood levels of both L-serine and D-serine and partially restored measures of fresh neuron production in the hippocampus. It did not improve the buildup of amyloid, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Importantly, this experiment tested L-serine and the production of new neurons, not D-serine supplementation as a treatment for human aging.

Recent findings suggest that taken together, these findings suggest that serine metabolism is a promising research target, but not a simple case of more being better. The form of serine, the condition being studied, and the outcome being measured all matter. Neither study directly confirms or overturns the original Menin results.

What the Findings Mean for People.

Industry observers note that there is some human research on D-serine, although it does not establish an aging treatment. A small randomized study published in 2016, before the Menin work, tested a single dose in 50 healthy older adults. Participants improved on one measure of a computerized maze task, but the researchers found no significant benefit on the other cognitive tests or mood measures. The experiment did not establish lasting memory benefits, slower aging, or the safety of prolonged use in older adults.

According to recent reports, the Menin findings leave several key questions unresolved. Researchers still need to determine what causes the protein to decline with age, how much of the resulting physical and cognitive deterioration can be prevented, and how long any benefits might last. They also need to understand whether altering Menin or supplementing D-serine could produce unintended effects.

The central possibility remains compelling: some changes associated with aging may be influenced by signals originating in a small part of the brain. Understanding those signals could reveal ways to protect function later in life. For now, however, the evidence points to an experimental pathway worth investigating, not a supplement proven to turn back human aging.

Brain’s Insula Shapes Pain, Emotion, and the Placebo Effect

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an international team of neuroscientists has mapped the functional architecture of the human insular cortex for the first time, revealing that it operates through four distinct yet cooperating subregions rather than as a passive sensory relay.
  • Source: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU).
  • Sources indicate that tucked deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the folds of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes lies the insular cortex, or insula, one of the human brain’s most enigmatic hubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an international team of neuroscientists has mapped the functional architecture of the human insular cortex for the first time, revealing that it operates through four distinct yet cooperating subregions rather than as a passive sensory relay. Drawing on 15 years of direct intracranial brain recordings across 87 epilepsy patients, the researchers uncovered a hierarchical network explaining how emotions and expectations actively reshape physical pain.

Source: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU).

Sources indicate that tucked deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the folds of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes lies the insular cortex, or insula, one of the human brain’s most enigmatic hubs. Serving as the primary meeting point where raw physiological signals from the body converge with emotion and conscious thought, the insula shapes everything from acute physical pain and temperature sensation to visceral anxiety and self-awareness.

Yet because of its deep anatomical location, mapping precisely where these distinct functions reside—and how they communicate—has long remained a major challenge in human neuroscience.

Recent findings suggest that now, in a landmark study titled “Functional architecture of the human insula,” an international team led by Dr. Julian Quabs and Professor Dr. Dr. Svenja Caspers at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) and Forschungszentrum Jülich (FZJ), working alongside collaborators at Stanford University and the National Research Council (CNR) in Parma, has created the first comprehensive functional atlas of the human insula.

To peer directly into the living human insula, the team analyzed intracranial electrophysiological data collected over roughly 15 years at Stanford University Medical Center from 87 patients undergoing diagnostic monitoring for drug-resistant epilepsy.

With patient consent, temporarily implanted depth electrodes allowed investigators to deliver targeted electrical stimulation across the insula while recording real-time sensations, neural activity, and directional connectivity with surrounding cortical networks.

This rare dataset revealed that the human insula is organized into four distinct, cooperating functional zones:.

Crucially, connectivity analyses revealed a powerful directional hierarchy: the cognitive insular pole exerts far stronger downward influence over the sensory rear regions than the sensory zones exert back onto the pole.

“Our findings show that the insula is more than a relay station for bodily signals. It appears to actively shape how we experience pain and our own bodies,” explained lead author Dr. Julian Quabs, who conducted much of the investigation during a research fellowship at Stanford University.

“This points to a possible neural mechanism through which emotions and expectations can alter how we perceive pain and other physical sensations,” added senior author Professor Dr. Dr. Svenja Caspers, Director of the Institute of Anatomy I at HHU and head of the Connectivity group at INM-1, FZJ.

By showing how top-down cognitive signals from the frontal lobe and insular pole directly modulate posterior pain-processing regions, the fresh atlas offers a concrete biological circuit underlying phenomena such as the placebo effect—providing a precise anatomical roadmap for future neuromodulation and chronic pain therapies.

What is the insular cortex (insula), and what does it do?

The insula is a region of cerebral cortex folded deep inside the brain that integrates physical signals from the body—such as pain, temperature, and heartbeat, with emotions and conscious awareness, shaping how we perceive both physical sensations and ourselves.

What are the four functional regions discovered in the new insula atlas?

Researchers divided the human insula into four cooperating zones: an upper rear region with a body-part map for pain and temperature; a lower region for widespread bodily sensations; a middle front region linked to chest/abdominal sensations and anxiety; and the front tip (insular pole), which connects to the frontal lobe to direct attention.

How does this study help explain the placebo effect?

The researchers discovered that the cognitive front tip of the insula (the insular pole) communicates strongly with the frontal lobe and sends powerful top-down signals to the pain-sensing regions at the back of the insula, showing how beliefs, expectations, and emotions can actively dial down physical pain.

Functional architecture of the human insula.

The insular cortex has a central role in pain, interoception and feelings, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood.

Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode.

Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception.

Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.

A study has found that decreasing about 47 grams of sugar intake per day — equivalent to a can of soda — lowers insulin secretion, on average, by 33 percent.

Increasing fibre intake by 5 grams a day — the amount in a half cup of beans — results in a 10 percent reduction of belly fat.

Visceral fat is a type of body fat stored within the abdominal area and internal organs.

This type of fat causes abdominal obesity and is also associated with several health problems, like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.

Dr Emily Ventura and colleagues conducted a 16-week study on overweight Latino adolescents who were between 12 to 19 years old.

They tested if increasing fiber consumption and decreasing sugar intake have an effect on type 2 diabetes risk factors.

“A reduction in visceral fat indicates a reduction in risk for type 2 diabetes, considering that to a greater degree than total body fat, visceral fat [fat surrounding the internal organs] has been shown to be negatively associated with insulin sensitivity.”.

According to recent reports, those who increased fiber intake had a significant reduction in body mass index (-2 percent vs. 2 percent) and visceral adipose tissue (-10 percent vs. no change) compared with those who decreased fiber intake.”.

Being overweight or obese are serious complications affecting adults and children around the world.

The World Health Organization reports that in 2016 over 1.9 billion adults were overweight and more than 650 million adults were obese.

The authors of this study wrote:.

“Our results suggest that intensive interventions may not be necessary to achieve modifications in sugar and fiber intake.

Accordingly, nutritional guidance given in the primary care or community setting may be sufficient to promote the suggested dietary changes in some individuals.

In addition, policies that promote reduced intake of added sugar and increased intake of fiber could be effective public health strategies for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in this high-risk population.”.

The study was published in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (Ventura et al., 2009).

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
  • Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels.
  • The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.

Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.

The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.

A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research.

For now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.

Recent findings suggest that over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.

It has been revealed that postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, notes one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.

"Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The new implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," says Kunyang Sui.

Recent findings suggest that sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.

Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers.

Brain researchers presently use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.

Conventional fibers, however, have an vital limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.

Industry observers note that the outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.

How the New Brain Implant Works.

The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.

A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.

Recent findings suggest that the finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be important because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.

In a recent development, the researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.

The experiments showed that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.

In a recent development, they were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.

Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience.

The in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.

Recent findings suggest that the research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.

How Young People Are Researching Problems That Matter to Them

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.
  • According to recent reports, middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code.
  • report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.

According to recent reports, middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities.

Many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students.

Research is one important way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate concerns, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers.

In schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR.

Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.”.

According to recent reports, systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access.

Relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this issue further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations.

According to recent reports, student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect fresh students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging.

Read more stories on our YPAR Hub.

In a recent development, our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods.

First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope.

Sources indicate that second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the challenges that students care about.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

According to recent reports, facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action plans and recommendations.

Finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or concern. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these concerns, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals.

YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters).

Further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an problem or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action plans and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action.

Throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, issue, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions intends and recommendations to address their selected problem.

According to recent reports, A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation.

You can learn more about YPAR practice and research by accessing the following resources: YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson aims and other resources YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here. IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson looks and other resources.

YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here.

IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

Industry observers note that the YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects.

Power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place.

Recent findings suggest that the results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action prepares.

One step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether new routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in.

Sources indicate that in our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued.

Sources indicate that there is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and New Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills.

It has been revealed that students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

#115597. Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (784 w)

Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • According to recent reports, to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • Sources indicate that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more notable problem: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

According to recent reports, to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

Sources indicate that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an important marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

Caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

Recent findings suggest that "Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," says Prof. Kurpas.

In practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

According to recent reports, "The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

Recent findings suggest that another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

"It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be notable," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

According to recent reports, caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

In a recent development, in that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

According to recent reports, "If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," claims Prof. Kurpas.

These findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

It has been revealed that "Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.

Blocking Gut Cannabinoid Receptors Restores Memory in Fragile X

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers demonstrated that selectively blocking peripheral cannabinoid receptors outside the brain improves memory, synaptic plasticity, and gut barrier integrity in fragile X syndrome mouse models.
  • Source: Pompeu Fabra University / Translational Psychiatry.
  • Fragile X syndrome is the most common single-gene cause of inherited intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers demonstrated that selectively blocking peripheral cannabinoid receptors outside the brain improves memory, synaptic plasticity, and gut barrier integrity in fragile X syndrome mouse models. Tthe study reveals that a one-week treatment restores beneficial gut bacteria and reverses hippocampal cognitive deficits without triggering central nervous system side effects.

Source: Pompeu Fabra University / Translational Psychiatry.

Fragile X syndrome is the most common single-gene cause of inherited intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder. Alongside cognitive impairment, memory deficits, hyperactivity, and autistic behaviors, individuals living with the condition frequently experience chronic gastrointestinal dysfunction, highlighting the intricate biological link between gut health and neurodevelopment. Despite decades of research, no targeted pharmacological therapies at the moment exist to treat the cognitive symptoms of fragile X syndrome.

Now, a study led by the Cognition Biology Research Group at Pompeu Fabra University (UPF) in Barcelona and published in Translational Psychiatry reveals that selectively targeting cannabinoid receptors outside the brain can simultaneously heal the gut microenvironment and rescue cognitive function.

In a recent development, led by principal investigator Dr. Andrés Ozaita alongside co-first authors Lucía de los Reyes Ramírez and Araceli Bergadà-Martínez, the research demonstrates that just one week of peripheral endocannabinoid inhibition reverses synaptic alterations in the hippocampus and restores intestinal barrier integrity in fragile X mouse models.

Industry observers note that the endocannabinoid system, particularly type 1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptors, plays a critical role in regulating synaptic transmission, neuroplasticity, and metabolism. Although CB1 receptors are roughly ten times more concentrated in the brain than in peripheral organs, drugs that broadly block central CB1 receptors often carry unacceptable psychiatric and neurological side effects.

To sidestep central nervous system risks, Ozaita and colleagues tested an experimental compound engineered to act strictly on peripheral CB1 receptors without crossing the blood-brain barrier.

In a recent development, “Unlike other drugs that act on the brain, the compound we have tested acts only on peripheral type 1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptors,” explained Ozaita, director of the Cognition Biology Research Group at UPF. “In the same way as in treatments that act on the brain, in mice with the fragile X mutation, this peripheral treatment enhances memory and increases plasticity, which improves the quality of neuronal connections in the hippocampus.”.

“Seeing that the results are comparable to those obtained using drugs that act on the whole body, we think that the main effect of broad-spectrum drugs is closely linked to their peripheral action,” Ozaita noted.

Because neurodevelopmental conditions frequently co-occur with gastrointestinal disturbances, the team examined how peripheral CB1 blockade influenced the gut microbiome and intestinal lining of fragile X mice.

Baseline analysis revealed pronounced gut dysbiosis and mucosal vulnerability in untreated fragile X mice:.

Following the one-week peripheral CB1 inhibitor regimen, both microbial balance and mucosal defenses rebounded.

“Peripheral pharmacological treatment helps restore the microbiome of mutated mice and increases the expression of the Muc2 gene. These two actions improve the ecosystem and the barrier of the large intestine,” said co-first author Lucía de los Reyes Ramírez.

“We cannot state that this recovery of the intestinal environment is due to the specific inhibition of the CB1 receptors in the intestine, but we can say that peripheral inhibition has a positive effect on the microbiota-gut-brain axis in mice carrying the fragile X mutation,” added co-first author Araceli Bergadà-Martínez.

By showing that cognitive rescue does not require drugs to directly penetrate the brain, and instead can be achieved by modulating the microbiota–gut–brain axis, the findings open a promising translational pathway for fragile X syndrome and related neurodevelopmental disorders.

Future studies will focus on pinpointing the exact signaling messengers linking peripheral CB1 inhibition to hippocampal synaptic remodeling, laying the groundwork for safer, targeted clinical trials in humans.

How can a drug that doesn’t enter the brain improve memory in fragile X syndrome?

According to recent reports, researchers at Pompeu Fabra University found that blocking peripheral type 1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptors outside the brain improves gut microbiome health and strengthens the intestinal barrier. These positive changes along the microbiota–gut–brain axis translate into healthier neuronal connections and improved memory in the brain’s hippocampus, without causing psychiatric side effects.

What gut abnormalities were found in fragile X syndrome models?

Mice with the fragile X mutation had lower levels of beneficial gut bacteria (Lactobacillus and Akkermansia) and reduced expression of the Muc2 gene, which produces the protective mucus barrier lining the large intestine.

Why is this discovery vital for developing human treatments?

In a recent development, currently, there is no approved medication to treat intellectual disability or memory impairment in fragile X syndrome, and drugs that block cannabinoid receptors inside the brain often cause adverse neurological side effects. Targeting peripheral receptors outside the brain offers a potentially much safer therapeutic strategy.

A serotonergic mechanism is involved in the pro-cognitive effect of AM6545 treatment in a mouse model of fragile X syndrome.

Recent findings suggest that fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the principal monogenic syndrome leading to inherited intellectual disability and autism. It is caused by the silencing of FMR1 gene that leads to the loss in the expression of its encoded protein, the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMRP). In synapses, FMRP has a key role in local mRNA modulation to maintain synaptic plasticity.

Recent findings suggest that the Fmr1 KO (FX) mouse model shows cognitive impairment and some of the synaptic traits present in individuals with FXS, together with alterations in gut microbiota. Previous studies revealed that pharmacological and genetic cannabinoid type-1 receptor (CB1R) inhibition significantly prevented central key alterations in FX mice. Here, we aimed to evaluate the effect of a sub-chronic treatment with the largely peripherally-restricted CB1R antagonist AM6545.

Sources indicate that we found that AM6545 reduced memory deficits and restored enhanced hippocampal mGluR5-dependent long-term depression and aberrant dendritic spine density in FX mice. At the peripheral level, AM6545 modified altered FX mice fecal microbiota composition and intestinal Muc2 expression, while in the hippocampus AM6545 treatment upregulated hippocampal Htr4, the gene encoding for serotonin receptor 4 (5-HT4R). This upregulation, also observed in cecum, positively correlated with memory performance. Notably, acute pharmacological blockade of 5-HT4R abolished AM6545 pro-cognitive effect.

Our results suggest that repeated peripheral CB1R inhibition ameliorates key central and peripheral alterations in FXS mouse model and modifies the expression of serotonergic receptors vital for cognitive performance. Together, this evidence points to the peripheral targeting of CB1R as an approach to alleviate cognitive dysfunction in the FXS context.

Feeling depressed can be a sign of vitamin B12 deficiency, a study finds.

People with a vitamin B12 deficiency are three times more likely to be experiencing ‘melancholic’ depression.

Melancholic depression mostly involves depressed mood.

Some of the other most common symptoms of depression are decreased interest in life or pleasure, energy loss and concentration problems.

The study also found a link between low folate intake and depression.

Folates include vitamin B9, folacin and folic acid.

People with a low intake of folates were 50 percent more likely to be experiencing melancholic depression.

The research included 2,806 Finnish people whose nutritional status and depression symptoms were assessed.

Although vitamin B12 and folates were linked to melancholic depression, the same link was not seen with non-melancholic depression.

Symptoms of non-melancholic depression cluster around anxiety and low self-esteem, with less emphasis on depressed mood.

Dr Jussi Seppälä, the study’s first author, mentioned:.

“The findings have practical implications in the care of patients with depressive symptoms.

For example, it may be wise to avoid medication causing weight gain among patients with non-melancholic depression, whereas melancholic depressive symptoms may call for a closer look at the quality of the patient’s diet.”.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is easy to rectify with supplements or by dietary changes.

The body uses vitamin B12 to make red blood cells and to keep the nervous system healthy.

Other common signs of vitamin B12 deficiency include experiencing muscle weakness and being constipated.

Meanwhile, some of the best dietary sources of folates include:.

Folate levels are particularly high in chickpeas, yeast extract, lentils and broad beans.

The study was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders (Seppälä et al., 2012).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recognizing the difference between a friend, a family member, and a stranger feels effortless to humans, yet it demands vast, specialized neural networks inside the primate temporal cortex.
  • It has been revealed that in a study published today in Cell, neuroethologists led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that researchers identified the specialized brain cells that allow Northern paper wasps (Polistes fuscatus) to recognize individual faces. The study reveals that despite evolving independently with brains the size of a grain of rice, paper wasps use neural population coding remarkably similar to that of primates and humans to distinguish facial patterns and navigate social hierarchies.

Recognizing the difference between a friend, a family member, and a stranger feels effortless to humans, yet it demands vast, specialized neural networks inside the primate temporal cortex. Astonishingly, an insect with a brain roughly the size of a grain of rice pulls off a remarkably similar feat.

It has been revealed that in a study published today in Cell, neuroethologists led by Dr. Christopher Jernigan, assistant professor of biology at Wake Forest University, alongside collaborators at Cornell University and Rockefeller University, identified for the first time the specialized group of neurons that enable the Northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscatus) to recognize individual wasp faces.

The discovery reveals that despite vast evolutionary distance and dramatically smaller neural circuitry, wasps and primates rely on strikingly parallel computational strategies to encode facial identity.

Recent findings suggest that found across eastern and central North America, female Northern paper wasps establish cooperative nests governed by strict linear dominance hierarchies. Rather than engaging in costly, exhausting battles every time they cross paths, nestmates rely on distinctive yellow, brown, and black facial markings to remember who outranks whom.

To uncover how the insect brain processes these visual cues, Jernigan, Cornell postdoctoral advisor Dr. Michael Sheehan, Cornell doctoral student Lorenz Mammen, and Rockefeller University neuroscientist Dr. Winrich Freiwald recorded neural responses while presenting wasps with images of other wasp faces.

The recordings pinpointed a dedicated group of brain cells tuned specifically to facial identity:.

It has been revealed that “These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” explained Jernigan, lead contact on the study. “These groups of neurons are all firing, and each neuron has a slightly different preference for one face or another.”.

This visual memory underpins remarkably sophisticated social cognition. Beyond recognizing established nestmates, paper wasps engage in social eavesdropping, observing fights between two unfamiliar wasps and remembering the outcome.

In a recent development, “They will treat the winner of that fight independently in a third interaction differently than they would the loser,” Jernigan said. “Despite having these small brains and relatively simple vision, they have these really complex social lives that revolve around this specialized ability to recognize each other.”.

Because the Northern paper wasp brain contains a fraction of the neurons found in mammals, it offers neuroscientists a tractable model system for tracing exact circuit wiring and studying how social experience sculpts visual recognition.

Supported by the National Institutes of Health and the National Eye Institute, Jernigan’s team next aims to investigate whether paper wasps can also read dynamic facial postures or expressions—offering deeper insights into the evolutionary rules that govern social perception across species.

“It’s really remarkable that they have this kind of really human-like or primate-like ability that you wouldn’t typically expect for an insect,” Jernigan noted. “And I think it’s almost unbelievable that they have some of the similar kind of neural computations for doing a similar task as we do. It takes a tremendous amount of neural connections to do something similar in a primate.”.

How can wasps recognize individual faces with such tiny brains?

Sources indicate that researchers discovered a specialized group of neurons in the Northern paper wasp brain that respond specifically to facial patterns. Much like human face-processing neurons, these cells fire in coordinated groups where each neuron is tuned to slight differences in facial markings and colors.

Why do paper wasps need to recognize each other’s faces?

Recent findings suggest that female Northern paper wasps live in colonies with strict social dominance rankings. Recognizing individual faces lets them remember who won previous fights and maintain social order without constantly battling their nestmates.

How does studying wasp brains help us understand human vision?

In a recent development, humans and wasps evolved facial recognition independently, yet both appear to use similar neural computation strategies. Because wasp brains are far smaller and simpler than primate brains, scientists can trace their exact neural connections to learn how visual experience wires the brain for social recognition.

Neural correlates of facial recognition in a social wasp.

In humans and other primates, faces are special visual objects that are encoded by circuits selective to faces. If specialized circuits are the most efficient way to encode and discriminate among similar-looking objects of high relevance, then we expect that analogous circuits should evolve in other taxa with specialized visual individual recognition abilities. Thus, we surveyed the neural responses to visual objects across the brain of a wasp that has independently evolved specialized facial recognition, Polistes fuscatus.

According to recent reports, we found a localized population of neurons analogous to face cells, which we term “wasp cells,” that selectively fire to front-facing wasp images. Some of these wasp cells encode information about facial patterns, which possibly underlie the unique visual recognition abilities of these wasps.

These findings demonstrate high-level feature-selective tuning in an invertebrate and suggest that specialized circuits are an adaptive feature for nervous systems requiring complex visual recognition.

Industry News: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • It has been revealed that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. Latest research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

It has been revealed that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh indicates.

The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

To explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions swiftly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

Recent findings suggest that the idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".
