Industry observers note that work can be tough. With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.

In a recent development, while some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace. For many years, researchers have been testing different practices that individual employees, managers, and teams can do to improve work life for everyone.

You can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being. Each practice includes:.

Recently, we added four fresh practices that you might want to try in your workplace.

Let’s face it: We don’t always feel appreciated at work, even though appreciation seems to be a key need for most people. In this practice, you begin a regular team meeting with the simple act of appreciating the person to your left. You say something specific about one of their qualities or an action they took and the impact it had on you. Then that person appreciates the person to their left, and you go around the room (or virtual meeting) until everyone gets appreciated.

It has been revealed that years ago, I tested this practice in a meeting with a team I was working with. When we got to the third person being appreciated, she broke down into tears. She stated, “I’ve been working here for nine years, and I didn’t know you guys appreciate me. . . . I didn’t even know you liked me.”.

Help everyone on your team feel appreciated to boost connection and performance.

It has been revealed that while this was hard to hear, it’s also a problem that is pretty easy to fix. Appreciation Circles, which can be repeated regularly, try to establish a culture and ritual of appreciation so that no one has to feel undervalued at work.

This practice is designed for managers during their regular (and sometimes less than inspiring) one-on-one meetings with their direct reports. It recommends that you ask employees these three questions:.

Industry observers note that as managers, sometimes we don’t realize the impact of our time with employees. Research suggests that our supportive behaviors can go a long way to helping employees feel more engaged. So how can managers be more supportive?

Improve employee satisfaction and engagement with a guided conversation.

Sources indicate that one study found that when managers encouraged, assured, and valued employee efforts, employees felt more engaged. These are the themes that the three questions in this practice address.

Industry observers note that the question of how you build trust has always been a fascinating one for me, because trust is so foundational to getting things done and is such an crucial part of a healthy workplace culture. Studies suggest that high-trust work cultures are often higher-performing, but how do you actually earn trust at work?

Recent findings suggest that in their analysis of hundreds of studies on trust, researchers found that there are three key levers for building trust: demonstrating your ability, benevolence, and integrity. In other words, people trust you more when they believe you can get things done, have their best interests at heart, and follow through on your word.

Demonstrate your trustworthiness to your coworkers.

This practice helps you identify ways to show others that you have these qualities by considering three questions and then acting on your answers:.

This practice is probably one of the more fun and feel-good practices because it encourages you to offer some random acts of kindness to your coworkers and see if this creates a multiplier effect in your workplace.

For example, you could bring a coworker a cup of coffee, help them with a project, or offer a handwritten thank-you note.

Do something nice for coworkers and watch kindness spread.

Studies suggest that kind and helpful behaviors can be contagious to those receiving the kind acts, and that even bystanders see boosts in their well-being just from observing these acts.

Industry observers note that we encourage you to try this low-risk and feel-good practice in your workplace soon—as well as the rest of them! Keep in touch and let us know how these practices land in your workplace.

Why We Slow Down With Age: Brain Serotonin Blocks Movement

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have uncovered the specific brain circuit responsible for age-related declines in physical activity.
  • Physical inactivity is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for chronic disease, frailty, and premature mortality.
  • In a fresh study published via ScienceDirect and supported by the UKRI-Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), researchers led by Professor Lora Heisler have identified a dedicated neurochemical circuit in the brain that actively dials down the natural drive to move as we grow older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have uncovered the specific brain circuit responsible for age-related declines in physical activity. The study reveals that aging increases serotonin signaling in motivation and movement centers, acting like a biological brake that suppresses dopamine-driven urges to move, while blocking this serotonin pathway restores youthful activity, speed, lean muscle mass, and grip strength in older mice.

Physical inactivity is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for chronic disease, frailty, and premature mortality. Yet across human populations and animal species alike, advancing age brings a predictable, progressive decline in spontaneous daily movement, a biological phenomenon whose root neural cause has remained largely unexplained.

In a fresh study published via ScienceDirect and supported by the UKRI-Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), researchers led by Professor Lora Heisler have identified a dedicated neurochemical circuit in the brain that actively dials down the natural drive to move as we grow older.

To establish how movement patterns shift across the adult lifespan, the research team first compared physical behavior in adults aged 50 to 70 against younger adults aged 17 to 30. Older adults walked more slowly, covered less daily distance, and carried higher levels of body fat, a behavioral and metabolic trajectory closely mirrored by aging mice.

Probing the neural circuits governing motivation and motor initiation in the mouse brain, the investigators uncovered a fundamental shift in neurochemical balance:.

“Think of the brain’s movement system as a bicycle. The brain chemical dopamine helps push the pedals, driving the urge to move, while another chemical called serotonin puts a brake on this pathway. With age, that brake becomes increasingly engaged, slowing voluntary movement. We found that releasing the brake restored more youthful levels of activity in older mice,” explained Professor Heisler.

“Rather than the aging brain running out of fuel, our findings suggest it may be applying too much brake. By reducing signalling through this serotonin pathway, we were able to release that brake and restore more youthful patterns of movement in older mice.”.

When the researchers experimentally blocked this age-amplified serotonin pathway in older mice, the physiological transformation extended well beyond increased step counts.

Releasing the neurochemical brake restored youthful spontaneous activity and movement speed, leading to measurable improvements in systemic physical health: treated older animals accumulated less body fat, gained lean muscle mass, and demonstrated stronger physical grip strength.

By demonstrating that age-related physical slowing is actively programmed by a modifiable brain circuit rather than inevitable muscular exhaustion, the research opens promising therapeutic avenues for extending healthspan and physical independence.

“Going forward, our findings suggest that targeting serotonin signalling in this pathway could one day provide new approaches to maintain mobility, independence, and healthy aging in an increasingly older population,” Heisler remarked.

“We all tend to slow down as we get older, but until now it hasn’t been clear why,” added Dr. Amanda Collis, Executive Director for Strategic Research and International at UKRI-BBSRC. “This BBSRC-supported research highlights that part of the answer lies in the brain, identifying a pathway that appears to dial down our natural drive to be physically active with age.”.

Why do people naturally become less physically active as they get older?

According to recent reports, researchers discovered that aging increases signaling in a specific serotonin pathway in the brain’s movement and motivation centers. This heightened serotonin acts like a brake that suppresses dopamine, the brain chemical that drives the natural urge to move, causing voluntary physical activity to slow down.

Can blocking this brain pathway reverse age-related slowing?

According to recent reports, in studies with older mice, blocking this overactive serotonin pathway released the biological brake on dopamine. As a result, older animals regained youthful levels of physical activity and movement speed, accumulated less body fat, gained lean muscle mass, and improved their grip strength.

What does this discovery mean for healthy aging in humans?

Because the decline in daily movement is driven by an active brain circuit rather than the body simply “running out of fuel,” targeting this specific serotonin pathway could eventually lead to newly introduced therapies that help older adults stay active, independent, and healthy longer.

Brain serotonin circuit reverses decline in physical activity with age.

Physical inactivity increases with age and is the fourth leading risk factor for mortality. Establishing the mechanisms underpinning declining activity with age has remained both elusive and difficult to overcome. Older (50–70 years old) compared with younger (17–30 years old) United Kingdom participants highlighted reduced physical activity, and this profile was effectively modelled in mice.

Analysis of brain serotonin neurons in the dorsal raphe (5-HTDR) revealed altered firing activity in older mice. Chemogenetically mimicking this 5-HTDR tone in young adult mice produced an older adult physical activity profile.

Genetically blocking 5-HT activity at 5-HT2C receptors prevented the decline in physical activity with age. Importantly, barring 5-HT action at 5-HT2C receptors specifically within the ventral tegmental area restored youthful physical activity levels and strength in older mice.

These data fill a longstanding knowledge gap by defining brain circuitry programming the decline in physical activity with age, and importantly, a means to reverse it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could correcting this vitamin deficiency make a difference for people already receiving treatment for depression?

Could correcting this vitamin deficiency make a difference for people already receiving treatment for depression?

Vitamin D supplements may ease symptoms in some people with depression, according to a review of the evidence.

Several small trials found improvements, including in people who started out with low vitamin D levels.

Other trials found little or no benefit, and one large study found that supplements did not lower the chances of developing depression.

The link is plausible because vitamin D may influence inflammation and chemical signalling in the brain, both of which are relevant to mood.

Depression itself could also lower vitamin D levels if it leaves people with less energy to go outdoors.

That makes it crucial to ask two separate questions: whether correcting a deficiency can help someone who is already depressed and whether taking vitamin D can prevent depression in the first place.

Researchers at the University of Oradea reviewed studies measuring vitamin D levels in people with and without depression, as well as trials testing whether supplements changed their symptoms.

One small trial recruited people who had both major depression and a vitamin D deficiency.

Both groups continued with their usual care, but after about three months, depression scores were lower in the group given a vitamin D injection than in the placebo group (Vellekkatt et al., 2020).

Differences in who took part, the doses they received and how symptoms were measured made the trials difficult to compare.

A trial designed to test prevention followed more than 18,000 adults aged 50 and over who had no clinically relevant depressive symptoms when they joined.

Over about five years, participants who took daily vitamin D were about as likely to develop depression or clinically relevant symptoms as those who took a placebo (Okereke et al., 2020).

Vitamin D receptors are found in parts of the brain such as the hippocampus, which is involved in memory and the response to stress.

The vitamin can also influence immune signals involved in inflammation.

This is one route through which it might affect mood in some people with depression.

Vitamin D levels also reflect habits that can change during depression, including what people eat and how much time they spend outdoors.

Someone who stops going for regular walks, for example, may get less sunlight and make less vitamin D as a result.

A blood test taken during an episode of depression cannot tell which change came first.

The question now is whether correcting a vitamin D deficiency can improve symptoms in people already receiving treatment for depression.

Answering it will take larger trials that recruit people with both conditions and follow them long enough to see whether any improvement lasts.

The study was published in the journal Pharmaceuticals (Roșian et al., 2025).

Recent findings suggest that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee may affect far more than alertness.
  • Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
  • The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee may affect far more than alertness. Newly introduced research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection.

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

Recent findings suggest that the new research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

What Happened When Coffee Was Removed.

The regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

It has been revealed that coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

Sources indicate that after coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects.

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

Coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Recent findings suggest that caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

Because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide fresh clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Recent findings suggest that corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet.".

According to recent reports, the findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," noted Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways.".

Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A latest study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques. The research shows that inhaled pollution reprograms the brain’s resident immune cells (microglia), compromises the blood-brain barrier, drains cellular energy reserves, and kills newborn neurons in the hippocampus.

Source: Case Western Reserve University.

Microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Mounting epidemiological evidence has also linked polluted air to cognitive decline, yet whether inhaled particles actively cause dementia, and precisely how they injure the brain, has remained an urgent scientific question.

Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.

According to recent reports, led by co-senior authors Dr. Sanjay Rajagopalan and Dr. Andrew Pieper, the research team combined population-scale human health tracking with controlled five-month inhalation experiments in mice to map the cellular chain reaction linking dirty air to dementia.

To quantify how long-term air pollution exposure shapes dementia risk across diverse genetic backgrounds, the researchers analyzed medical and environmental records from roughly 500,000 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank, tracked for up to 14 years.

Even after controlling for confounding variables, including age, smoking status, diabetes, and socioeconomic factors—people residing in the most polluted third of geographic regions were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia than those living in the cleanest third. Crucially, high air pollution elevated dementia risk regardless of whether an individual carried high or low inherited genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

To test causation directly, the investigators exposed mice to real-world outdoor Cleveland air for five months, concentrating PM2.5 particles to match levels recorded in the world’s most heavily polluted urban centers.

Even in otherwise healthy mice without genetic predispositions to neurodegeneration, chronic PM2.5 exposure triggered widespread brain pathology:.

Recent findings suggest that remarkably, these memory deficits and Alzheimer’s-like cellular injuries emerged in healthy mice completely devoid of amyloid plaques. When the researchers exposed mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s pathology to the same polluted air, the particles inflicted identical neuroinflammatory and metabolic damage while simultaneously accelerating amyloid plaque accumulation.

“By recreating in mice what happens when people breathe polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” explained Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine. “These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it.”.

It has been revealed that “We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” added Pieper, director of the Harrington Discovery Institute Brain Health Medicines Center and psychiatrist at the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center. “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors.”.

How much does air pollution increase the risk of developing dementia?

In an analysis of nearly 500,000 adults tracked for up to 14 years, researchers found that people living in areas with the highest levels of fine particulate air pollution were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias than those in the cleanest areas, even among people with low genetic risk.

What does fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) physically do to the brain?

In mouse experiments recreating urban air pollution, inhaled PM2.5 particles caused the blood-brain barrier to leak, triggered brain inflammation, lowered cellular energy reserves (NAD+/NADH ratio), killed newborn memory neurons in the hippocampus, and reprogrammed the genes of the brain’s immune cells (microglia).

Does air pollution only harm brains that already have Alzheimer’s plaques?

Sources indicate that no. Researchers were struck to find that air pollution caused memory problems, immune cell disruption, and neuron death in healthy mice that had no amyloid plaques at all, while also speeding up plaque buildup in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer’s disease.

Air pollution exposure interacts with Alzheimer’s genetic susceptibility to reshape microglial epigenomic and transcriptional programs.

Chronic exposure to fine particulate matter air pollution (PM2.5) is associated with cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease, but the biology connecting inhaled particles to the brain remains incompletely defined. Among 475,325 eligible UK Biobank participants, long-term PM2.5 exposure and Alzheimer disease (AD) polygenic risk were both independently associated with higher risk of AD and related dementias (ADRD).

The PM2.5-by-polygenic risk score (PRS) interaction in Cox models was statistically significant but sub-multiplicative or below unity (interaction HR 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.998; p = 0.026), indicating that the combined association was smaller than the simple product of the two individual associations.

To define the underlying biology, we exposed 5xFAD mice, an amyloid-based model of AD, and wild-type (WT) littermates to concentrated ambient PM2.5 or filtered air for 20 weeks. PM2.5 exposure activated microglia, disrupted the blood-brain barrier, depleted the brain NAD+/NADH pool required for resilience and repair, impaired postnatal hippocampal neurogenesis, and caused cognitive deficits.

Sources indicate that in 5xFAD mice it additionally increased amyloid burden. Paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of microglia isolated from the same animals demonstrated that exposure remodeled both gene expression and chromatin accessibility, and that that magnitude and direction of this response depended on genotype, converging on inflammatory, lysosomal, oxidative-stress, synaptic, and amyloid-related pathways.​.

​These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice​ support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure.

Latest Update: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone.
  • Recent findings suggest that newly introduced research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces.
  • In a recent development, researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide important clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

Recent findings suggest that newly introduced research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

In a recent development, researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

Recent findings suggest that "Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," said Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable.".

Following Children's Attention Over Time.

Sources indicate that earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

It has been revealed that the Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

In a recent development, "The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," stated Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before.".

It has been revealed that the research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of Newly introduced Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

During each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face demonstrated a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Sources indicate that children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

Family History Changes the Pattern.

The results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an important role.

Recent findings suggest that among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb said.

Sources indicate that "We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair said. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions.".

Happy Faces May Lose Their Pull.

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb mentioned.

The distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

According to recent reports, the researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak. The study shows that listening and speaking neurons sit side by side, opening latest targets for neurosurgical mapping, autism research, and brain-computer interfaces that restore speech.

For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.

Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.

Now, in a landmark study published in Science, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) led by neurosurgeon Dr. Edward Chang have resolved that 150-year-old puzzle.

Drawing on 15 years of high-resolution intracranial brain recordings alongside targeted neural experiments, the team demonstrated that a specialized hub within Wernicke’s area actively generates a cognitive “blueprint” for each word roughly a quarter-second before a person begins to speak.

According to recent reports, in the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke originally speculated that the posterior temporal lobe housed an “auditory image of words”, an internal template that could guide spoken output. Over subsequent decades, however, because the region sits nestled inside auditory cortex, neuroscientists largely pigeonholed it as purely a passive receiver for incoming speech sounds.

Recent findings suggest that “What’s different now is that we finally have the tools and the data to see the brain at the speed and scale at which speech actually happens — millisecond by millisecond, down to individual neurons,” explained co-first author Dr. Matthew Leonard, associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF.

Combining longitudinal intracranial recordings gathered in Chang’s laboratory with new experiments designed to separate listening from speaking, Leonard and co-first author Dr. Alex Silva, a student in UCSF’s Medical Scientist Training Program, pinpointed a crucial cortical hub: the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG).

Tracking neural activity at millisecond resolution revealed that specific populations of neurons inside the lpSTG surged into action approximately 250 milliseconds (a quarter-second) before vocalization began.

Crucially, this pre-speech firing did not represent raw acoustic sounds or physical movements of the lips and tongue. Instead, lpSTG neurons constructed an abstract linguistic blueprint encoding:.

It has been revealed that once assembled in the lpSTG, this structural blueprint traveled forward to speech-planning networks in the frontal lobe, and subsequently to the motor cortex, which translated the plan into precise articulatory muscle commands. Furthermore, high-resolution mapping showed that neurons dedicated to hearing speech sit directly beside, and sometimes overlap with, the neurons generating outgoing word blueprints.

“This changes the textbook view of how the brain perceives and produces speech,” mentioned Chang, chair of the UCSF Department of Neurological Surgery and member of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences. “Instead of being separate systems, the processes of hearing speech and actually speaking are very intertwined.”.

Housing incoming auditory processing and outgoing word planning inside the same microcircuit provides a compelling neural mechanism for how infants acquire language, converting heard sounds directly into motor-ready speech blueprints. It also offers a targeted anatomical region to investigate why roughly one-quarter to one-third of autistic children remain minimally verbal despite demonstrating strong language comprehension.

“It gives us a specific place in the brain to look, and a specific question to ask,” Chang noted.

Equally transformative are the implications for neurotechnology. Today’s speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) typically decode intended words from the motor cortex, a strategy that fails if a patient’s motor pathways are severely damaged. Because the lpSTG operates upstream of motor execution, it offers an alternative decoding gateway.

In proof-of-concept testing with two participants living with severe paralysis and anarthria (inability to speak), the UCSF team successfully decoded both the words participants attempted to say and the words they heard directly from lpSTG signals, pointing toward future conversational BCIs capable of capturing both sides of human dialogue.

How does this discovery change what we know about how the brain produces speech?

For over 100 years, textbooks taught that speech comprehension (Wernicke’s area) and speech production were handled by separate brain systems. UCSF researchers proved that a region inside Wernicke’s area (the lpSTG) actually activates a quarter-second before we speak to build an abstract “blueprint” of each intended word, including its length and syllable count, before sending it to motor areas.

Why can damage to Wernicke’s area make it hard to speak words, not just understand them?

Because the neurons that process heard speech sit directly alongside the neurons that build the structural blueprint for spoken words in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, a stroke or injury to that region disrupts both language comprehension and word planning.

How could this finding help paralyzed patients communicate?

Sources indicate that current speech brain-computer interfaces read signals from the brain’s motor cortex, which can be damaged in some paralyzed patients. Because the lpSTG creates word blueprints earlier in the speech pipeline, decoding signals from this region could restore communication for a wider range of paralyzed individuals—and potentially capture both heard and spoken words for natural conversation.

A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area.

In a recent development, wernicke’s area, located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the human brain, has long been considered essential for understanding speech. However, damage to this region also disrupts the ability to produce speech, creating a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience. Traditional explanations propose that this area primarily supports speech production indirectly by monitoring sounds during speaking. However, it remains unclear whether this region plays a more direct role in generating speech itself, and if so, what kind of information it represents: sounds, movements, or even properties of whole words. Resolving this question is critical for understanding how the brain constructs language and for developing technologies to restore speech in individuals who have lost it.

Addressing this question requires probing the human brain at multiple scales with both correlational and causal methods. We combined several complementary approaches, including high-resolution direct recordings of neural populations and single neurons during speaking and listening, electrical stimulation of specific brain regions to test causality, and analysis of patients with localized brain lesions. Across these methods, participants performed a variety of speaking and listening tasks ranging from naturalistic speech to single word repetition, providing a detailed and holistic view of the role of the posterior temporal lobe in generating upcoming speech.

In a recent development, we identified a specific subregion within individual participants’ Wernicke’s area—the left posterior superior temporal gyrus—that becomes active before speech begins. This early activity precedes word onsets in continuous speech rather than reflecting feedback from hearing one’s own voice. Brain stimulation and lesion analyses showed that disrupting this region causes errors in speech production, confirming its causal role.

Detailed analyses revealed that this region encodes properties of entire words, such as their length and frequency, rather than individual sounds or motor movements. This is distinct from neighboring brain regions that encode auditory feedback and do so by representing lower-level features such as articulation or sound.

Timing analyses indicated that activity in this region occurs earlier than in motor areas responsible for controlling speech muscles, placing it at the start of the speech production process. Recordings from individual neurons further confirmed that cells in this region respond before speech production, respond selectively to specific words, and are active during both speaking and listening.

Finally, in people unable to speak due to paralysis, signals from this region could be used to decode both intended and perceived speech, demonstrating its potential for multimodal brain-computer interface technologies aimed at restoring communication.

According to recent reports, this work identifies a specialized region within Wernicke’s area that generates word-level representations before speech is produced. Rather than serving primarily as a center for speech perception, this region acts as an early stage in the production process, organizing upcoming words before they are translated into motor commands. These findings resolve a long-standing paradox about Wernicke’s area and provide a unified framework for understanding how the brain links language comprehension and production. They also highlight a promising target for future neuroprosthetic devices aimed at restoring speech in individuals with communication impairments.

Self-Objectification Alters Brain Response to Media

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women.
  • Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.
  • Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women. The findings suggest that internalized beauty standards reshape how the brain regulates and evaluates objectifying media.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.

While behavioral studies have established that self-objectification heightens sensitivity to media portrayals, precisely how a woman’s self-perception alters the underlying neural circuitry that evaluates sexualized visuals has remained unclear.

In a study published today in eNeuro, a research team led by Zhennan Liu at Shanghai Normal University and Haoyue Qian at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated how individual differences in self-objectification shape both subjective beauty judgments and brain responses to sexualized imagery.

The investigators recruited 60 healthy cisgender heterosexual female participants with an average age of approximately 20 years. First, the team assessed each participant’s baseline level of self-objectification using a validated psychological scale measuring how strongly individuals prioritize external appearance over internal bodily competence.

Next, participants viewed and rated a series of photographs categorized by the researchers as either:.

While participants across the board rated the sexualized photographs as more attractive than the non-sexualized images, women with higher self-objectification scores assigned significantly higher attractiveness ratings to the sexualized visuals.

When the team examined the accompanying brain activity, they uncovered a striking neural signature: women who scored higher on self-objectification exhibited dampened neural activity in brain regions involved in aesthetic judgment while assessing sexualized images.

Rather than heightened analytical engagement, this reduced activation suggests an altered regulatory or automatic evaluative response when processing culturally idealized, objectifying imagery.

“Differences between individuals [in this study] may come from how their brains regulate and evaluate the attractiveness of these images,” explained Qian.

By connecting self-objectification to measurable shifts in aesthetic evaluation circuitry, the study illustrates how internalized social standards leave a functional footprint on visual and emotional processing.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to move beyond observational associations to test whether psychological training can buffer the brain against objectifying media.

In a recent development, “We want to test whether experimentally training or manipulating regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal) can change how women respond to and rate sexualized images,” Qian remarked. “This will help move the work from association toward causal and intervention-relevant questions.”.

What is “self-objectification,” and how did researchers measure it?

Self-objectification is the tendency to view and judge one’s own body primarily from an outside observer’s perspective, prioritizing physical appearance over internal physical capabilities. Researchers measured this trait using a validated psychological questionnaire before participants viewed media images.

How did self-objectification affect brain responses to sexualized images?

Women with higher self-objectification scores rated sexualized images of women as significantly more attractive than peers with lower scores, and revealed dampened brain activity in regions responsible for aesthetic judgment, indicating differences in how their brains regulate and evaluate beauty standards.

Could psychological strategies change how the brain reacts to objectifying media?

Researchers hope to test whether training cognitive regulation techniques, such as cognitive reappraisal, which helps people consciously reframe how they interpret visual stimuli, can modify brain activity and reduce vulnerability to sexualized media representations.

Trait Self-Objectification Modulates Attractiveness-Regulating Neural Activity in Sexual Objectification Processing: An ERP Study.

Contemporary mass media frequently emphasize women’s sexual attractiveness, thereby perpetuating sexual objectification and exacerbating mental distress. Trait self-objectification is presumed to be a risk factor for these adverse outcomes; however, the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying individuals’ responses to sexual objectification remain poorly understood.

In a recent development, the present study examined how trait self-objectification modulates behavioral and electrophysiological responses to sexualized female images. Behaviorally, sexualized portrayals of women increased attractiveness ratings, and this enhancement was further modulated by individual levels of trait self-objectification. Neurally, processing sexualized female images evoked a set of ERPs indexing early neurocognitive processes, including perception-related N170 and EPN, and attention-related P200.

Distinct later neural responses were also identified, including the emotion-related centro-parietal LPP and the regulation-related frontal LPP (f-LPP). Among these sexual objectification-related ERP components, only the f-LPP was modulated by trait self-objectification.

Furthermore, follow-up analyses revealed that the degree to which trait self-objectification increased individuals’ attractiveness ratings of sexualized images was associated with their reduced f-LPP activity.

Collectively, these findings suggest that trait self-objectification modulates the processing of sexually objectifying stimuli by altering neurocognitive processes underlying attractiveness regulation, highlighting the importance of this regulatory mechanism in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

The cultural emphasis on women’s sexual attractiveness perpetuates sexual objectification, which is associated with adverse mental health outcomes. Trait self-objectification may modulate these outcomes, yet its relationship with the processing of sexual objectification remains unclear. This study found that trait self-objectification shapes attractiveness ratings during sexual objectification processing.

Although sexualized images elicited multiple neurocognitive components—N170 and EPN (perception-related), P200 (attention-related), cp-LPP (emotion-related), and f-LPP (regulation-related)—individual differences in trait self-objectification were selectively associated with f-LPP activity. These findings highlight the potential role of attractiveness-related regulatory processing in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

Tech Report: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine.
  • Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age.
  • Industry observers note that to investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

Industry observers note that to investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations.

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI indicated the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

It has been revealed that addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions.

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

It has been revealed that one area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which demonstrated higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

According to recent reports, addiction indicated a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

A Potential Source of Future Biomarkers.

It has been revealed that the findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide new clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions.".

Industry observers note that this work was supported by the Key Research and Development Proposal of Jiangsu Province, China (BE2023668) to S.Q., and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62376124) to S.Q. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

#115582. Why Sending Reels Is More Meaningful Than You Think

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1642 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Why Sending Reels Is More Meaningful Than You Think

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Humans are constantly reinventing ways to maintain intimacy with the people we care about most.
  • In a recent development, this has been my experience.
  • Sources indicate that A couple of years ago, we started sending each other reels through Facebook (her preference) and Instagram (my preference).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Humans are constantly reinventing ways to maintain intimacy with the people we care about most. Today, one of our most ubiquitous connection rituals is reel sharing—that is, sending short social media videos to each other. At a time when much of the conversation about technology centers on how it is eroding human connection, reel sharing and the unspoken social norms that surround it suggest another possibility: a tool to maintain social bonds.

In a recent development, this has been my experience. I met my best friend of more than 25 years, Kyra, when I was a Peace Corps volunteer. Our friendship formed before social media and with geographic distance between us (she served in Togo and I was in Cameroon). During Peace Corps service, we mainly stayed in touch through sporadic emails. After Peace Corps, we both started careers in international development, got married, and had a few kids. Our geographic separation didn’t change, but our time to email and chat on the phone did, significantly limiting our communication. I missed her.

Sources indicate that A couple of years ago, we started sending each other reels through Facebook (her preference) and Instagram (my preference). It became our version of “I’m thinking of you” or “Here’s something to brighten your day”—an asynchronous way of staying connected, sharing our interests, and quietly checking our emotional attunement with one another. Sending reels has helped to strengthen our friendship at a cadence that works for our busy lives.

In a recent development, but there’s a tension with this practice, which is the guilt I sometimes feel about spending so much time on social media. Though an estimated 37–71% of Americans use social media sites, many have turned against them altogether, inviting us to throw out both the baby and the bathwater. Indeed, the parent manufacturer of Facebook and Instagram (Meta) recently settled a lawsuit (for billions of dollars) that alleged that their sites were intentionally designed to addict children and teens.

According to recent reports, there might be good reasons to restrain social media use, but people will continue to use it—and so the question becomes: How can they use it wisely? Perhaps repositioning social media reel sending as a ritual of connection can help to recalibrate how and why we engage with the platform.

Recent findings suggest that social science sees interpersonal rituals as repetitive, symbolic actions that foster belonging and communicate shared meaning. Such rituals are routinized actions or behaviors that have unspoken norms understood by the participants. Performing the ritual with others symbolizes their importance in our lives and creates an opportunity for shared meaning, which collectively reinforces the bond.

Sending reels has become a modernized form of relationship maintenance, done to keep a relationship alive, relevant, and emotionally present. Relationship maintenance is a behavior we engage in to show our commitment to a relationship. There are both routine and strategic forms of relationship maintenance. We employ these tactics across all types of relationships: romantic, platonic, familial, and professional.

Routine maintenance consist of frequent, intuitive acts done to stay connected to the person through regular communication and information sharing—as opposed to grander gestures like buying flowers and other gifts, showing up at difficult moments, or bringing someone to the airport.

It has been revealed that the reason we feel irritated when our reel sending doesn’t receive a reaction is because relationships are rooted in social exchange. Essentially, relationships are based on a subconscious cost-benefit analysis, where reciprocity is expected, although not explicitly stated. Behaviors that are rewarded will continue—but the absence of reward can harm the relationship.

Sources indicate that perhaps you’re a mom who recently started sending reels to your adult daughter to reinforce regular communication. You’ll likely continue to do so until you realize, “Wait, she hasn’t responded.” While the action of sending reels is something we may do without much thought, we expect acknowledgment of the gesture: a like, emoji, comment, or reciprocal sending. When we don’t receive that, we feel disappointed. But when we do get the anticipated response, we feel closer to the person.

Kyra and I use a combination of emojis and reciprocal sending to signify reception. We’re so committed to reciprocal sending, that the other day she sent me this reel to remind me what to do if a couple of days went by without her sending me anything!

Think about the last person you sent a reel to. Who was it? I’m willing to bet they were a close friend, relative, or romantic partner. That’s because reels are typically shared with someone you care about, someone you want to be in community with, and the goal is to reinforce closeness.

While research focused on sending reels as a form of digital communication is scarce, we can extrapolate the link between relationship closeness and reel-sending behavior from studies focused on digital memes (static photos) and GIFs (looping animations).

According to recent reports, researchers asked 395 study participants, ranging in age from 18 to 75, to recall situations where they sent a text message to a strong tie (close relationship) and a weak tie (acquaintance) and report their use of graphic icons such as memes, GIFs, and emojis. Participants reported more sharing with strong ties than weak ties.

Those who used graphic icons more frequently reported greater feelings of self-disclosure (“I can talk to X about anything”), relationship maintenance (We “try to make each other laugh”), and intimacy (“How often do you tell your friend everything that you are going through?”).

Admittedly, sending a reel to someone requires a bit of vulnerability.

You are taking a risk by sending something that resonates with you, but you aren’t 100% sure will resonate and be reciprocated by the other person. The likelihood of success depends on how accurately you guessed the person’s likes or dislikes.

Sources indicate that the vulnerability factor is another reason we are more likely to send reels to close others; vulnerability typically follows closeness, not the other way around. When we are vulnerable with people we are close to, the risk is diminished because we know them better. If it fails, the potential harm is cushioned by our established relationship.

Industry observers note that aside from the vulnerability factor, there’s a reason when you’re scrolling social media that you don’t see a reel and immediately think to send it to Bob in accounting or your dentist. While they may be cool people, they simply aren’t top of mind for you.

It has been revealed that close relationships carry emotional weight, and our brain is much more likely to remember emotionally salient information. For example, Kyra has three very active sons who all play competitive sports. Her weekends are consumed with sporting events, so every time I see a post about sports moms, I think of her and send it. It’s my way of recognizing her efforts and sacrifice.

Recent findings suggest that reels are digital objects that can trigger us to think of others. Because we have much more information about close relationships and cognitively our experiences with them are more accessible, when we want to share a reel, we pick from this list of people.

In a recent development, shared experiences are an crucial component of fostering connections, serving as the foundation for establishing shared meaning. When you’re in the same physical space, this might look like watching movies together, attending events, or sharing meals.

It has been revealed that reels offer an asynchronous substitute for shared experiences. By viewing a reel, and maybe even sharing a brief commentary on it, and then sending it to a connection who then reacts, you are creating a digital shared experience—viewing and reacting to the same content.

Shared experiences help us to understand the preferences and thoughts of others, while sharing our own. Through this exchange, we can align our minds and create shared meaning. It’s a form of emotional attunement, a core component of close social connection.

Sending reels tests out that alignment. Essentially, when we send reels, we are saying, “I found this to be funny, did you?” or “This really resonated with me, how about you?”  or “I thought this information would be useful to you, is it?” The validation of alignment is in the receiver’s reaction.

When distance or busyness prevent or limit in-person interaction, sending reels allows us to share funny, thought-provoking, or motivational content with people we care about, maintaining a sense of closeness, having laughed, gasped, or become angry at the same reel. We reinforce connection through mutual understanding and shared meaning.

Sources indicate that if you send reels and you’ve categorized it as a “guilty pleasure,” I’d encourage you to reconsider the guilt part. Guilt suggests you are doing something bad when the intention and the value behind sending the reel is likely anything but.

The all-or-nothing culture of social media today doesn’t give space for a more nuanced look at our productive use of these platforms and overlooks that some of our online engagement reflects values-based behaviors.

Sources indicate that the question is not simply how much time we spend on social media, but what we are doing there. Compulsive scrolling and intentionally connecting with someone we care about may occur on the same platform, but they are not the same.

Industry observers note that so, keep sending the reels, not as the only sign that you care, but as one of many in your interpersonal toolbox. I know Kyra and I don’t proposal on stopping anytime soon!

Sources indicate that shanna B. Tiayon, Ph.D., also known as “The Wellbeing Dr.,” is a writer, speaker, and trainer working in the area of well-being. Right now, Shanna is the owner of WellbeingWorks, LLC, a boutique well-being firm bringing together the best interdisciplinary knowledge in the areas of social psychology, human resources, research, and training design.

Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable.
  • Recent findings suggest that parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it.
  • Yet a fresh psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable. Three experiments reveal that while cognitive effort improves comprehension, it does not spark curiosity or enjoyment, instead, preexisting interest motivates students to engage in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it. Behind this common wisdom lies an intuitive assumption that sustained cognitive effort naturally blossoms into curiosity and intrinsic motivation.

Yet a fresh psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.

Industry observers note that published in Acta Psychologica, the study demonstrates that forcing effort improves basic comprehension, but it does not make dry or unappealing material more interesting. Instead, genuine interest and liking come first—serving as the psychological spark that motivates learners to invest cognitive effort voluntarily.

It has been revealed that “I’m curious if a student is made to work harder, does that bring the same benefits as effort they choose to give,” asked Yimeng Jin, a doctoral student at Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Systems Life Sciences and first author of the study. “It matters because many learning environments rely on required effort, such as assignments, on the assumption that more effort is always better.”.

To disentangle voluntary motivation from mandatory mental exertion, Jin and senior author Professor Johan Lauwereyns at Kyushu University’s Faculty of Arts and Science conducted three behavioral experiments involving 110 university students.

In a recent development, participants read pairs of seemingly unrelated sentences and decided whether they wanted to construct an explanation connecting them. By tracking participants’ initial choices, task completion, and time spent, the team isolated two distinct components of learning: willingness to engage and cognitive effort invested.

Across the three experimental phases, a clear cognitive pattern emerged:.

According to recent reports, “Interestingly, participants who were required to explain spent more time on the task than those who chose to do so,” Jin noted. “Perhaps they initially skipped it because the sentences were harder to understand, so they needed more time to make sense of them. It’s a bit like struggling through homework in a subject you don’t enjoy. Together, the experiments suggest that effort can help people make sense of information, while interest is more closely linked to their willingness to engage.”.

In a recent development, while the researchers caution that short laboratory reading tasks among university students differ from long-term classroom learning in younger children, the findings carry broad implications for how educators, parents, and communicators design learning environments. Rather than relying solely on mandatory drill work to manufacture enthusiasm, sparking authentic curiosity first may unlock deeper, faster comprehension.

According to recent reports, “The findings have implications far outside education. The connection between engagement and effort is key whenever our understanding depends on reading texts,” concluded Lauwereyns.

Does working harder on a subject automatically make it more enjoyable?

No. Researchers at Kyushu University found that while putting in cognitive effort helps students better understand difficult material, it does not increase their interest in or enjoyment of the subject.

What actually motivates students to put effort into learning?

In a recent development, the experiments showed that preexisting interest and liking come first. When students already find a topic intriguing, they are far more willing to engage voluntarily, and they comprehend the material more efficiently than when forced to work through topics they want to skip.

What happens when students are forced to work on material they don’t find interesting?

When participants were required to explain material they initially chose to skip, they spent significantly more time struggling with the task, gained less comprehension compared to voluntary effort, and demonstrated no increase in enjoyment.

Effort enhances understanding, while appreciation drives engagement in Cross-sentence semantic processing.

Comprehensive reading requires active semantic processing, going beyond explicitly stated information to construct connections and meaning. Building on discourse coherence theory, Reader-Response Theory and insights from Language Poetry, the present research investigates how active engagement and cognitive effort shape semantic processing.

We propose that evaluative dimensions central to aesthetic appreciation, namely understanding, interest, and liking, also play vital roles in semantic processing.

To examine these processes, we developed a novel cross-sentence elaboration paradigm using unconnected, randomly paired sentences that create semantic gaps and encourage reader-driven meaning construction.

In a recent development, in Experiment 1, participants could voluntarily invest effort by thinking aloud during elaboration. Results showed greater volitional engagement was associated with higher levels of understanding, interest, and appreciation.

Experiment 2 dissociated willingness to engage from actual effort, revealing that appreciation predicted participants’ willingness to invest further effort, whereas additional completed effort did not consistently increase appreciation.

Experiment 3 examined forced effort, showing that externally imposed effort enhanced semantic understanding but did not consistently increase appreciation, highlighting the distinct roles of volitional and imposed effort.

An integrated 2 × 2 analysis of Experiments 2 and 3 showed that active engagement and cognitive effort made distinct, interactive contributions to evaluation and processing time, with completed cognitive effort more reliably predicting accurate recognition memory and active engagement more closely tied to memory for the processing context.

Together, these findings clarify the interplay between engagement, effort, understanding, and appreciation, offering latest insights into the cognitive dynamics of active meaning construction in semantic processing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A small preliminary study from UC San Francisco adds to mounting evidence that eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help reduce symptoms of depression.

Published Sept. 23 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study was funded by the National Institutes of Health. Researchers believe it is the first study to compare depression symptoms in the same participants before and after they moved from their usual ultra-processed diet to healthier foods.

The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, stated it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial.".

Depression Symptoms Improved After a Major Diet Shift.

It has been revealed that participants cut their intake of ultra-processed foods by more than 85%. After doing so, they indicated moderate to large improvements across three different measures of depression. Anxiety scores also improved modestly.

Ultra-processed foods include products such as packaged snacks, fast food, sugary drinks, and other industrially manufactured foods. These products may contain ingredients including preservatives, artificial coloring, flavor enhancers, and emulsifiers.

In a recent development, "Reducing the amount of ultra-processed food in our diet can be challenging, because it's highly palatable, cheap, and convenient," noted corresponding author Nyasha Chagwedera, MD, PhD, assistant professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. "Ultra-processed food triggers dopamine, the pleasure hormone, which promotes craving. Food companies work with scientists to find just the right amount of sugar, salt, and fat that make you want to eat more and more.".

Testing the Gut-Brain Connection.

Industry observers note that the participants had an average age of 44, and 70% were female. Along with depression, 14 participants also had anxiety. Everyone in the study had a high BMI and at least one metabolic disorder -- such as hypertension, diabetes, or elevated LDL cholesterol.

Recent findings suggest that researchers divided the participants into two groups. One group stayed on its usual diet for four weeks, while the other switched to a diet low in ultra-processed foods. Participants selected and bought their own food with guidance from the research team. After four weeks, the groups switched diets.

Chagwedera, who founded the UCSF Metabolic and Mental Health Program, said one possible explanation for the connection between ultra-processed food and depression involves what she described as a "leaky, out-of-balance gut." According to this idea, ultra-processed foods may damage the protective lining of the gut.

"This gut damage can create low-grade, chronic inflammation throughout the body that either directly causes depression or makes people more vulnerable to it.".

"In other words, junky processing may harm your gut in ways that ripple up to your brain.".

Larger Depression Trial Planned.

Because the study was small, the findings are still preliminary. The researchers now blueprint to investigate the effect in a larger group, with enrollment for phase 2 expected to begin in 2028.
